facts.statement: The genus Megacephalosaurus was described by Schumacher and colleagues in 2013.
facts.quote: authority: Schumacher et al., 2013

facts.statement: The genus name refers to its large head, which is the largest among North American plesiosaurs and measures up to 1.75 meters long.
facts.quote: It is named after its large head, which is the largest of any plesiosaur in the continent and measures up to 1.75 m in length

facts.statement: Its long snout and uniform teeth suggest it fed on smaller-sized prey.
facts.quote: Its long snout and consistently sized teeth suggest that it preferred a diet of smaller-sized prey

facts.statement: The first fossils of Megacephalosaurus were discovered in 1950.
facts.quote: First discovered in 1950

facts.statement: Fossils have been found in the Carlile Shale and Greenhorn Limestone in Kansas and other parts of the midwestern United States.
facts.quote: The fossils have been found in deposits of the Carlile Shale and Greenhorn Limestone in Kansas and elsewhere in the midwestern United States

facts.statement: The first specimen was discovered on June 5, 1950, by teenage brothers Frank and Robert Jennrich.
facts.quote: The first specimen of Megacephalosaurus was discovered on June 5, 1950 by two teenage brothers named Frank and Robert Jennrich

facts.statement: The initial discovery consisted of a skull preserved upside down and crushed into a thin layer.
facts.quote: Their discovery consisted of a skull preserved bottom-side up and completely crushed into a thin layer

facts.statement: Paleontologist George F. Sternberg initially identified the fossil's locality as likely being the Greenhorn Limestone or Graneros Shale.
facts.quote: Sternberg identified the locality to likely be either the Greenhorn Limestone or Graneros Shale

facts.statement: Sternberg originally identified the holotype specimen (FHSM VP-321) as the pliosaur Brachauchenius lucasi.
facts.quote: Sternberg identified FHSM VP-321 as the Late Cretaceous pliosaur Brachauchenius lucasi

facts.statement: After consulting with other paleontologists, Sternberg identified the specimen as the Late Cretaceous pliosaur Brachauchenius lucasi.
facts.quote: Sternberg identified FHSM VP-321 as the Late Cretaceous pliosaur Brachauchenius lucasi

facts.statement: In November 2003, Robert Jennrich led museum staff back to the original discovery site to re-examine the locality.
facts.quote: In November 2003, Robert Jennrich led staff members of the Sternberg Museum to the original locality where he and his brother discovered the specimen

facts.statement: Scientists determined the fossil came from the Fairport Chalk Member of the Carlile Shale, dated to approximately 92.9 million years ago, rather than the Greenhorn Limestone or Graneros Shale.
facts.quote: Scientists found that this locality was not of the Greenhorn Limestone or Ganeros Shale as Sternberg initially presumed, but instead of the Fairport Chalk Member of the Carlile Shale, dated approximately 92.9

facts.statement: Museum curator Mike Everhart found photos of the skull's underside showing features distinct from other Brachauchenius lucasi skulls.
facts.quote: Mike Everhart discovered photos of the skull's underside taken prior to its mounting, which revealed underside features that were different from those found in other B. lucasi skulls

facts.statement: A 2013 study concluded that the skull possessed unique features making it a distinct genus separate from Brachauchenius lucasi.
facts.quote: The study, which was published in 2013, found the skull bore several unique features that made it distinct from B. lucasi and concluded that FHSM VP-321 was a distinct genus of pliosaur

facts.statement: The genus name Megacephalosaurus combines Greek words for "great," "head," and "lizard" to reference the skull's large size.
facts.quote: It was named Megacephalosaurus eulerti, with the generic name being a portmanteau of the Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, "great") and κεφαλή (kephalḗ, "head") prefixed onto σαῦρος (saûros, "lizard") in reference to the size of the skull

facts.statement: The species name eulerti honors Otto C. Eulert, who donated the fossil specimen.
facts.quote: the specific epithet being an honor of Eulert for his donation of the fossil

facts.statement: Matrix tests from a paratype skull indicated nannofossil assemblages associated with the Greenhorn Limestone, dating the specimen to at least 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: tests on a piece of matrix extracted from the fossil identified nannofossil assemblages that are most associated with deposits of the Greenhorn Limestone likely dated around 93.9 mya at earliest

facts.statement: Museum curator Mike Everhart suggested that two other Kansas skulls labeled as Brachauchenius lucasi might actually belong to Megacephalosaurus.
facts.quote: In a blog post, Everhart suggested that two partial fossil skulls from Kansas, currently labeled as B. lucasi, may actually belong to Megacephalosaurus

facts.statement: A skull cataloged as UNSM 112437, found in the Graneros Shale during Glen Elder Dam construction, may be the oldest known specimen of the taxon.
facts.quote: the second skull, catalogued as UNSM 112437, comes from the Graneros Shale and was discovered during the construction of Glen Elder Dam in Mitchell County, being possibly the oldest known specimen of the taxon

facts.statement: Only two fossil specimens of Megacephalosaurus are currently known.
facts.quote: Two specimens pertaining to Megacephalosaurus are known.

facts.statement: The second known specimen, USNM 50136, is designated as the paratype.
facts.quote: The second specimen, USNM 50136, is designated as the paratype specimen.

facts.statement: Megacephalosaurus possesses the largest known plesiosaur skull from North America.
facts.quote: The skull of Megacephalosaurus is the largest known for any plesiosaur from North America to date.

facts.statement: The holotype skull measures 150 cm in cranium length and 171 cm in lower jaw length.
facts.quote: FHSM VP-321 measures 150 cm in length when measuring along the midline of the cranium and the length of the lower jaw measures 171 cm.

facts.statement: The paratype specimen is estimated to have had a skull length of 175 cm when complete.
facts.quote: UNSM 50136, although incomplete, is much larger than FHSM VP-321 and is estimated to have measured 175 cm when it was complete.

facts.statement: Based on skull size comparisons, Megacephalosaurus likely had a total body length between 6 and 9 meters.
facts.quote: This would yield a range of 6-9 m in total body length for Megacephalosaurus.

facts.statement: The snout of Megacephalosaurus is very elongate, comprising about two-thirds of the total skull length.
facts.quote: The snout is very elongate, making up around two-thirds of the total skull length.

facts.statement: Unlike other pliosaurs, the maxillary teeth of Megacephalosaurus remained consistently large and did not reduce in size towards the back of the skull.
facts.quote: Unlike in pliosaurs such as Liopleurodon or Pliosaurus, the maxillary teeth in Megacephalosaurus do not reduce in size towards the base of the skull and are all consistently large.

facts.statement: The lower jaws of Megacephalosaurus bear twenty-three pairs of functional teeth.
facts.quote: The lower jaws bear twenty-three pairs of functional teeth.

facts.statement: The largest teeth in Megacephalosaurus reach approximately 4.5 cm in crown height.
facts.quote: The largest teeth known in Megacephalosaurus measure up to approximately 4.5 cm in crown height.

facts.statement: The tooth enamel features apicobasal ridges that run from the crown base to the tip.
facts.quote: The enamel features patterns of long, thin, and convex ridges known as apicobasal ridges that run in the direction from the crown base to tip.

facts.statement: Researchers propose that apicobasal ridges on the teeth helped improve gripping and puncturing prey.
facts.quote: The function of apicobasal ridges in the teeth has been proposed to be to improve gripping and puncturing prey.

facts.statement: The ribs of Megacephalosaurus are double-headed, allowing attachment at two points on a vertebra.
facts.quote: However, ribs of Megacephalosaurus are double-headed, meaning that the head of the rib is structured for attachment at two points of a vertebra.

facts.statement: Double-headed ribs are a unique feature among Cretaceous pliosaurs, as all other species lack them.
